title: Hiring: Founding AI Engineer
summary: Help build the AI systems changing how construction projects get priced and built.
body_text: Apply for this role About Alkali Alkali is an AI-native price estimation and 3D-modeling platform for construction. We’re changing how construction projects are built in the U.S. Today, steel fabricators estimate the price of multimillion-dollar projects by reviewing paper blueprints with a highlighter. Alkali uses computer vision, VLMs, and agents to produce faster, more accurate estimates. Each month, steel fabricators across the United States use Alkali to estimate hundreds of projects covering millions of pounds of steel. By volume, more than ~10% of U.S. structural steel flows through our platform. About the Role We are hiring a founding AI engineer to help own Alkali’s core AI systems. You will develop and optimize: Vision Models: Improve vision models that extract components, quantities, annotations, schedules, and geometry from engineering drawings. Agents: Build agents that navigate large plan sets, use specialized tools, and complete complex estimating and engineering workflows. Data and Evaluation Pipelines: Develop the datasets, pipelines, and harnesses to optimize system performance and understand failures. About You You have: Trained and evaluated computer vision models Designed data schemas and labeling ontologies Built and maintained large-scale data and model pipelines Built and evaluated agents with complex tool sets The ability to take ownership outside your existing specialty and quickly learn unfamiliar domains, including engineering drawings and construction workflows Why Alkali You will work directly with the founders, own a broad portion of the AI stack, and see your work used on real construction projects. You will work with unusually rich visual and geometric data, help shape Alkali’s technical direction, and build systems that influence how physical infrastructure gets priced and built. title: Resideo Showcases Strength, Innovation and Profitable Growth Opportunity at Investor Day
summary: Resideo leaders outlined the company's profitable growth strategy, innovation roadmap and competitive advantages during Investor Day at the New York Stock Exchange.
body_text: Summary At Resideo's 2026 Investor Day, company leaders shared how innovation, operational excellence and financial discipline are driving long-term value creation. Presentations highlighted the company's unique position in the home, strong market-leading brands, connected home opportunities, and plans for sustainable growth and profitability. Resideo Showcases Strength, Innovation and Profitable Growth Opportunity at Investor Day Presentations spotlighted the competitive advantages, durable demand and connected home opportunities that set Resideo apart. Company News Leadership 7/21/26 Resideo hosted its Investor Day at the New York Stock Exchange on July 13, 2026, ahead of the planned spin-off of ADI Global Distribution. The company's incoming leadership team provided in-person attendees and the live webcast audience a look at Resideo's strategy, product innovation, and how the company delivers comfort and protection to millions of homes and businesses around the world. "When you combine our footprint in the home, our durable market position and our competitive position with the focus that will come from being a standalone company, we believe Resideo is uniquely positioned to win," said incoming President and Chief Executive Officer Tom Surran. "We believe the strategy and operational excellence we've been discussing today allow us to target revenue growth and sustained margin expansion even without a significant improvement in the economic environment." The Resideo Investor Day presentation and video replay is available at Investor.Resideo.com . Connecting the home, driving growth, and creating value The event also featured comments from Senior Vice President of Engineering Scott Ziffra, Senior Vice President of Sales and Marketing Scott Harkins, Senior Vice President of Integrated Supply Chain and Information Technology Patrick Murray, and Global Head of Strategic Finance Christopher Lee. "We're standing here at the New York Stock Exchange for an incredibly profound moment for Resideo," said Lee. "We hope you walk away today with a better understanding of Resideo and share our conviction about the opportunities for Resideo to be the leader in residential sensing and controls." Accelerated development of differentiated solutions "We don't just build products; we understand how homes actually work. That understanding becomes our data, our insight, and ultimately our advantage," said Ziffra. "We're building a home that understands, anticipates, and acts. And ultimately, this connected ecosystem, connectivity, platform, intelligence, it doesn't just add value. It creates a durable, compounding advantage that's very difficult to replicate." Continued focus on the pro "I can say with conviction, I have never been more excited about our future than I am right now," Harkins said. "We have built long-term, trusted relationships with over 100,000 pros globally ... Resideo is a long-term growth story. It's built on the pro, it's scaled globally, and it's positioned to compound value for both our customers and our investors." Leveraging scale to provide superior value "Our manufacturing strategy has strengthened product quality, improved supply chain resiliency, and increased our speed of execution," Murray said. "Everything we have done has been centered on one thing, speed. Speed in manufacturing, speed in the flow of information, and speed in decision-making. These strengths enable us to deliver the industry-leading performance that defines Resideo today." Resideo rings the Closing Bell at the NYSE The day concluded with Resideo leaders ringing the NYSE Closing Bell to mark the opportunities ahead for the company, and its professional installers and integrators, partners, and employees. Times Square billboard highlights Resideo Resideo's Investor Day events in New York City also included a digital billboard in Times Square, at the corner of West 47th Street and 7th Avenue. Images of the banner and Closing Bell courtesy of NYSE Group. title: A nation that adapts: What 60 years of Barclaycard, the UK’s first credit card, tells us about how Britain pays
summary: 2026 marks 60 years since Barclaycard became the UK’s first credit card, and Maria Sienkiewicz, Head of the Barclays Archive, reflects on how it reshaped payments and what that journey reveals about the future
body_text: A nation that adapts: What 60 years of Barclaycard, the UK’s first credit card, tells us about how Britain pays UK UNLOCKED 2026 marks 60 years since Barclaycard became the UK’s first credit card, and Maria Sienkiewicz, Head of the Barclays Archive, reflects on how it reshaped payments and what that journey reveals about the future. This article is part of our UK unlocked series - expert insights on the economic and business issues most critical to the UK's companies and policy leaders. Visit our UK unlocked hub Maria Sienkiewicz, Head of Barclays Archive Read time: 4 minutes Barclaycard launched the UK’s first credit card on 29 June 1966, with over 1 million customers signing up within its first year The introduction of credit cards marked a step-change in financial independence, enabling many women to access credit in their own name without a male guarantor Early adoption followed a familiar pattern: initial scepticism, card returns and uncertainty, followed by rapid mainstream uptake Barclaycard processed the UK’s first electronic card payment in 1986 at a Miss Selfridge store in Brent Cross, transforming retail transactions The business went on to pioneer contactless payments in the UK and introduce mobile and wearable payment technologies, making transactions faster and increasingly invisible Contactless now dominates behaviour, accounting for 66% of all UK credit card transactions Today, there are around 59 million credit cards in circulation in the UK, with 419 million transactions worth £23.8 billion recorded in a single month (March 2026) Britain has always had a quiet talent for adapting to change, and no story tells that better than how we pay. As Head of the Barclays Archive, I spend my days immersed in the materials that trace this evolution, from handwritten records and customer correspondence to the various wonderful marketing campaigns, internal strategy papers and the artefacts of everyday banking life. Payments may seem routine, even invisible, but in the archive, they tell a richer story: one of shifting expectations, changing social norms, and, crucially, growing independence. 2026 marks the 60th anniversary of Barclaycard, the UK’s first credit card, which launched on 29 June 1966. At the time, the idea of paying with a piece of plastic rather than cash or cheque challenged so many long-held assumptions about money. And what began as a modest initiative, a six-page strategy, £20,000 of investment and a team of just 200 people working from a converted shoe factory in Northampton, quickly became something larger. Within 12 months, more than one million people had signed up. That early adoption reflects something enduring about Britain: when a new way of doing things proves useful, people are willing to adapt and to do so quickly. A key driver of financial autonomy For many people, the credit card was about far more than convenience. It marked a subtle but significant shift in financial independence. The launch of the credit card marked the moment when people could quickly and easily access credit. No more uncomfortable interviews with the Bank Manager. This was a huge change for everyone, but especially for women, who had often had to provide a male guarantor before credit was agreed. Women were no longer just seen as household purchasers, but as individuals managing their own credit and financial decisions. It is a reminder that innovation in payments does not simply alter transactions; it reshapes who is able to participate fully in economic life. The practicalities of this shift are equally striking. “How to use your Barclaycard” guides carefully walk customers through a system that was entirely new. Today, payments innovation is often intuitive; in 1966, it had to be explained step by step. These documents speak to the effort required to build trust and to a public willing to learn. A slow burn Adoption was not immediate. As Patricia Lancaster, an original Barclaycard employee recalled to me, many recipients initially returned their cards, unsure what they would use them for. In the archive, traces of that uncertainty remain, letters, forms and queries from customers encountering something unfamiliar. Yet what followed is a pattern repeated over decades: scepticism gives way to understanding and understanding to widespread adoption. Behind the scenes, the systems powering these early transactions were equally revealing. Patricia described a workplace driven by paper, punch cards and a single “giant” computer – - far removed from today’s real-time digital environment. Yet even then, the foundations of modern payments were being laid: fraud prevention processes, transaction tracking and the operational discipline needed to grow securely. Over time, novelty became habit. Through the 1970s and 1980s, credit cards moved from occasional tools to everyday essentials, supported by expanding merchant networks and rising confidence. By the time electronic payments, Chip & PIN and contactless technology arrived, the behavioural groundwork had already been established. Barclaycard also played a pivotal role in accelerating that technological shift. In 1986, it installed the UK’s first electronic point-of-sale terminal at a Miss Selfridge store in Brent Cross, processing the country’s first in-store electronic card payment, a transaction that marked the beginning of faster, more efficient retail payments. From there, it continued to pioneer new ways to pay, leading the rollout of contactless technology in the UK in 2007 and later introducing mobile and wearable payments, helping to move transactions ever closer to being seamless and invisible within everyday life. Today, contactless is the UK consumer’s most popular way to pay, accounting for 66% of all credit card transactions. A total transformation Today, that transformation is unmistakable. There are now 59 million credit cards in circulation in the UK, and, in March of 2026, the most recent month on record with UK finance, there were 419 million credit card transactions with a total spend of £23.8 billion. But the innovation has not stopped. In 2025, for the second consecutive year, Barclaycard onboarded more than one million new customers. While forms have evolved, from plastic cards to phones, wearables and increasingly invisible payments, the demand for convenience, control and security remains constant. From an archival perspective, that is perhaps the most powerful insight: payments innovation is never only about technology. It is about people, who they are, what they value, and how their roles evolve. Moments of pressure have often accelerated that evolution. Economic uncertainty, shifting consumer confidence and, more recently, the pandemic have all driven rapid behavioural change - from the rise of contactless to the growth of digital-first transactions. Each time, the same pattern emerges: necessity drives experimentation, and experimentation becomes habit. A time of change Looking back to 1966, the launch of Barclaycard formed part of a wider moment of national change. The BBC was preparing to introduce colour television, England would go on to win the World Cup, and new consumer experiences were reshaping everyday life. It was a period defined by optimism and innovation and by a willingness to embrace the new. That instinct endures. As payments become more seamless, more embedded and often less visible from biometric authentication to AI-driven systems - the pace of change is only accelerating. Yet the lesson of the past 60 years is clear: while the technology evolves, Britain’s capacity to adapt remains constant. From a single card issued from a converted factory to a sophisticated digital ecosystem, Barclaycard’s history is not just a story of innovation. It is a story of a society learning, adjusting, and democratising payments to make them accessible for all. And if the archive tells us anything, it is this: how Britain pays will keep changing, and it will be shaped not just by technology, but by the people who choose to adopt it. title: How Do Handoff AI Takeoffs Compare to Buildxact Takeoffs?
summary: Buildxact's Blu AI assists your takeoffs. Handoff AI does them for you. Compare automation, cost, and turnaround to pick the right takeoff software.
body_text: Buildxact takeoff software and Blu AI: What it does Buildxact is a strong residential construction estimating platform with a full pre-construction suite: takeoff, estimating, proposals, change orders, and a client portal. It's been around long enough to build real credibility in the residential builder space, and its pricing integrations are useful. Buildxact's Blu is an AI layer across the platform with four core modules: Blu Takeoff Assistant: AI-assisted scaling and measurement that preps your takeoff faster Blu Estimate Reviewer: AI double-checks your estimate for missed items and common errors Blu Assembly Assistant: AI support for building repeatable estimate assemblies Blu Estimate Generator: creates an estimate framework you then refine Blu reduces friction in the estimating workflow and helps catch mistakes. But here's the critical detail: Blu is positioned as an assistant . It preps and speeds up the work while you stay at the desk to review, edit, and build the estimate. Blu assists. You execute. Pricing caveat for Buildxact One more detail worth knowing before you compare pricing: on Buildxact's Foundation and Pro plans , Blu's AI tools are paid add-ons. The full Blu suite comes standard only on the top-tier Master plan. AI that helps you costs extra as you go. Factor that into the comparison. The difference between an AI Assistant and an AI Agent for takeoffs There's a reason the industry distinguishes between AI assistants and AI agents . An assistant helps you do something. An agent does it for you. When you use Buildxact's Blu to scale your blueprint and guide your measurements, you're still clicking through plans. You're still reviewing AI suggestions and confirming them one by one. The cognitive load is lower. The time savings are real. But you're still in the workflow, making decisions, validating outputs. For contractors with dedicated estimators, this is valuable. The estimator's job gets easier and faster. For contractors without a dedicated estimator (or for busy GCs who just need the takeoff done) assistance isn't the same as automation. Buildxact's Blu AI works alongside you as an assistant — it helps, prompts, and assists as you move through the measurement process. Handoff's AI works instead of you as a teammate — upload your plans, and it handles the entire takeoff autonomously. Handoff AI Takeoffs: Automate the takeoff that connects to your estimate and proposal Handoff AI doesn't assist. It executes. You upload your residential construction plans up to 5,000 sqft and walk away. In under 2 hours, the AI delivers: A color-coded visual takeoff PDF of every room with area, length, and count measured and marked A written summary of scope and quantities, ready to turn into an estimate Material quantities priced against 60M+ SKUs from major suppliers (Home Depot, Lowe's, etc.) ZIP-code level regional pricing for your market, not a national average No measuring. No clicking. No sitting with the plans. And when it's done, the color-coded PDF lets you check every measurement before the estimate goes out. Autonomous doesn't mean out of your control. Handoff was trained on 100,000+ completed residential estimates . It recognizes floor plans, elevation drawings, and plan sets the way an experienced estimator would, because it has processed thousands of real residential projects across every trade and scope type. Comparison: Buildxact Takeoffs vs Handoff AI Takeoffs Which platform should you pick for your takeoffs? If you have estimating staff and want to make their workflow smarter — Buildxact's Blu is a solid option. If you're a solo contractor, a small GC, or a growing remodeling company that wants takeoffs done without dedicating staff hours to them — Handoff AI is a different category entirely. Takeoff software helps you measure faster. Handoff AI does the measuring for you. For contractors whose time is their most valuable asset, that difference is the whole decision. Other FAQs about Handoff takeoffs and Buildxact takeoffs Should I choose Buildxact or Handoff AI for takeoffs? Choose Buildxact if you have estimating staff and want AI that makes their workflow faster. Choose Handoff if you want the takeoff done without staff: upload plans and get back a complete, color-coded takeoff in about two hours. The cost structure differs too, since Blu's full suite requires Buildxact's top tier while AI Takeoffs come included with Handoff Scale plans . Do I have to switch platforms to use Handoff AI Takeoffs? No. Handoff works alongside whatever workflow you run today, so you can use AI Takeoffs without migrating your projects or retraining your team. Contractors who want everything in one place can also run their estimates, proposals , contact records, and invoices in Handoff. Do AI takeoffs work for remodels or only new construction? Both. Handoff was trained on more than 100,000 completed residential estimates, which include kitchen remodels, bathroom additions, and whole-home renovations alongside new builds. Any residential plan set up to 5,000 square feet works.

title: The $180M Lesson: When the Perfect Resume Fails
summary: The market knowledge your talent decisions depend on — centralized. Verata unifies company intelligence, executive data, and search management in one platform built for PE talent and executive search.
body_text: The $180M lesson has direct implications for how PE firms approach CEO selection, onboarding, and evaluation: Evaluate situational fit, not credential fit. Before launching a CEO search, define the three to five specific operating capabilities the portfolio company needs in the next 18-36 months. Then evaluate candidates against those capabilities -- not against a generic template of what a "great CEO" looks like. CEO #1 was a great CEO in the abstract. CEO #2 was the right CEO for this specific situation. Take internal candidates seriously. The reflexive preference for external hires with impressive resumes over internal candidates with deep context is not supported by the data. Internal promotions succeed for reasons that credential-based screening cannot capture: institutional knowledge, team relationships, product understanding, and customer proximity. Your VP of Product or VP of Operations may be a stronger CEO candidate than the external search delivers -- and at a fraction of the transition cost. Structure your first 90-day evaluation around leading indicators. The $180M case would have been identifiable within 90 days if the board had been evaluating CEO #1 against specific operating milestones rather than giving the benefit of the doubt to an impressive resume. Three missed quarters is 9-12 months of value destruction that could have been mitigated with earlier intervention. Build a feedback loop. Track the relationship between CEO selection criteria and actual portfolio outcomes across your fund. Most PE firms have never systematically analyzed whether their hiring criteria predict their exit outcomes. When they do, they will find what the data shows at scale: the criteria are not working. The gap between the precision of your return expectations and the imprecision of your CEO selection criteria is where value is being destroyed. The $180M lesson is not about one company or one CEO. It is about an industry-wide selection model that is systematically miscalibrated -- and the returns that are being left on the table as a result.

title: NetBase Quid Alternatives for 2026: 8 Tools Compared on Video Coverage, Pricing, and Reviews
summary: NetBase Quid is a strong enterprise intelligence platform with one real gap — it can't see video. Compare 8 alternatives on coverage, pricing, and reviews.
body_text: Most "NetBase Quid alternatives" roundups treat this like a straightforward feature swap: list five or six enterprise listening tools, note that they're all quote-only, done. What they miss is the question that actually separates these vendors: which ones still just read text, and which ones can watch or listen to a video? That gap matters more every quarter. A growing share of brand conversation now happens as something a creator says out loud or holds up to the camera — never typed into a caption, bio, or hashtag. NetBase Quid, by its own reviewers' account, already misses a meaningful share of Instagram and TikTok posts at the text level. Whether its true replacement needs to fix that, or needs something else entirely (deeper historical archives, a bundled CX suite, research-grade rigor), depends on which problem is actually yours. Here's what NetBase Quid actually does well, where its real gaps are, and how eight alternatives — including one genuinely surprising finding about which competitor quietly became video-capable via partnership — compare on coverage, pricing, and reviews. What NetBase Quid actually does well (and where it falls short) NetBase Quid started as two separate companies: NetBase, founded in 2004, built social-listening and sentiment tooling; Quid, Inc., founded in 2010 with early backing from Peter Thiel's Founders Fund, built network-visualization and text-analytics tooling. The two merged in January 2020, and the combined company rebranded again to simply "Quid" in 2023 — then relaunched its product architecture as the "Q Platform" on February 25, 2026, adding an AI agent layer called AskQ with its own MCP connector for enterprise LLM integration (Source: Quid — Q Platform Press Release, 2026 ). Third-party review sites still list it as "NetBase Quid," which is the term this piece uses throughout — but it's worth knowing the company itself has moved on twice since the merger. The product has real strengths. It's rated 4.3/5 on G2 (305 reviews) and 4.6/5 on Capterra (43 verified reviews), with network and topic visualization — mapping how topics, influencers, and brands connect — cited as a genuinely distinctive feature most listening tools don't match. Its own homepage positions it as ingesting "more than 2 petabytes of data" across social platforms, news, patents, investment data, and product reviews (Source: Quid — Homepage, 2026 ), and named customer results circulating in third-party case-study aggregators include 7-Eleven, StarKist, and Coca-Cola — though a direct fetch of Quid's own case-studies page returned a 404 this session, so treat those figures as third-party-aggregated rather than freshly vendor-confirmed (Source: CaseStudies.com — NetBase Quid, 2026 ). Its real, reviewer-confirmed gaps are narrower and more specific than most comparison posts suggest. NetBase Quid publishes no pricing anywhere; third-party estimates range from roughly $4,995 per quarter at entry to $30,000 or more per year at enterprise scale, with no self-serve tier or free trial at any level (Source: SelectHub — Quid Reviews, 2026 ). And its discovery layer — confirmed directly by its own reviewers — "misses a lot of posts from key platforms such as IG and TikTok" (Source: Capterra — Quid Reviews, 2026 ). Sentiment accuracy is another recurring complaint: one reviewer notes the tool "analyzes the sentence and not the paragraph," missing broader context even when individual lines are read correctly. Why teams look for NetBase Quid alternatives Three sourced, independent reasons recur, and only one of them is really about video. Quote-only, enterprise-sales-cycle pricing with no self-serve path. NetBase Quid requires a sales conversation for any figure at all, and reviewer-cited entry costs of $20,000 or more per year put it out of reach for teams that want to test before an annual commitment — a friction point it shares with Brandwatch, Synthesio, and Digimind, but not with YouScan or Syncly Social. Confirmed coverage gaps on exactly the platforms where brand conversation is growing fastest. Health and beauty alone accounts for 79.3% of TikTok Shop sales, generating more than $1.34 billion annually (Source: BeautyMatter — TikTok Live Beauty, 2025 ) — and NetBase Quid's own reviewers say its scraper already misses a meaningful share of posts on Instagram and TikTok specifically, at the text level, before video-content understanding even enters the picture. Ingestion that remains text- and metadata-first, even after the February 2026 AI-agent relaunch. Q Agents and AskQ add a natural-language query layer over the platform's existing data — they don't add speech-to-text transcription or on-screen visual detection inside video content. A creator who names a product on camera without ever typing it anywhere stays invisible to that search, the same as before the relaunch. How we evaluated these alternatives Every vendor below was assessed against the same honest standard used throughout this series: does it have real, named customer evidence, and how does its actual discovery mechanism work — not just what its marketing claims? The results were genuinely uneven. Synthesio, an Ipsos company not usually included in "NetBase Quid alternatives" roundups at all, turned out to be the one enterprise peer in this tier that quietly became video-capable via a January 2026 partnership — a finding that undercuts the lazy assumption that every text-first enterprise tool in this category lacks video entirely. Vendor Named-customer evidence Video/visual capability Assessment NetBase Quid (Quid) Strong, third-party-aggregated: Coca-Cola, 7-Eleven, StarKist, Chevrolet, others (not independently re-verified on Quid's own site) None confirmed — text/metadata ingestion + Feb 2026 AI-agent query layer Genuinely strong network-visualization and predictive-analytics platform with real, reviewer-confirmed cost and coverage-gap friction Syncly Social Anonymized performance results (90% faster setup, 970K+ mentions analyzed) per internal benchmarks Native — audio transcription + on-screen visual/logo detection across TikTok, Reels, YouTube Shorts by default Video-native by design; the only vendor here built specifically around untagged spoken and on-screen mention detection Brandwatch Enterprise breadth (1.7 trillion historical conversations back to 2010) Publicly roadmapped for 2026, not yet shipped Real depth and history; don't claim shipped video-AI parity with Meltwater, Synthesio, or Syncly Social Talkwalker Enterprise-grade, platform-generic Non-gated Blue Silk AI speech-to-text + video-logo recognition, included at every tier Real video/audio AI breadth, not confirmed as TikTok/Reels/Shorts-specific Meltwater Named beauty/consumer customer stories: Shiseido, Yves Rocher, Bon Parfumeur Genuine TikTok video transcription via TikTok Marketing Partners integration Strongest combination of named-customer proof and confirmed video AI among enterprise peers researched in this cluster Sprinklr No specific named case study independently located None confirmed — AI+ Studio focuses on comment summarization, not video understanding Largest, priciest all-in-one CX suite; discontinued self-serve entirely as of April 2026 Synthesio (Ipsos) No specific named case study independently located; G2 4.3/5, 151 reviews Genuinely surprising: January 2026 ViralMoment partnership adds real scene/logo recognition and TikTok transcripts The one alternative here (besides Syncly) with confirmed, dated video intelligence — via partnership, not native Digimind (Onclusive Social) No specific named case study independently located None confirmed Budget end of the enterprise tier; same parent company found weak on public customer proof when researching Determ alternatives YouScan No specific named case study independently located Image recognition + YouTube-specific audio monitoring for spoken mentions Real visual and partial-audio capability at a materially lower price than every other vendor here; audio is YouTube-only, not cross-platform The 8 best NetBase Quid alternatives in 2026 1. Syncly Social Best for: brands and consumer-insights teams whose customers talk about them out loud or hold products up to the camera inside TikTok, Instagram Reels, or YouTube Shorts videos — conversation NetBase Quid, and most enterprise consumer-intelligence tools, cannot see at all. Where NetBase Quid's own reviewers confirm its scraper already misses posts on Instagram and TikTok at the text level, Syncly's video analysis transcribes spoken audio and detects on-screen text and logos inside past videos, surfacing brand mentions a creator never typed anywhere. That same engine powers competitor tracking built around actual content, not just handle mentions — and, in a detail worth noting given NetBase Quid's own new AI-agent layer, Syncly ships its own MCP connector for pulling this data directly into enterprise LLM workflows. Pricing: custom — book a demo (see below for a free trial link). 2. Brandwatch Best for: teams that want NetBase Quid's enterprise scale plus the deepest historical and forum archive researched in this comparison — 1.7 trillion historical conversations reaching back to 2010, with broad language coverage to match. Pricing: no public list price; comparable public estimates place entry tiers around $800-$2,000/month, scaling to enterprise custom quotes (Source: Vendr — Brandwatch, 2026 ). Its own 2026 roadmap lists "deeper analysis of video and image content" as a forward-looking goal, not a shipped feature (Source: Cision/Brandwatch Press Release, 2025 ) — don't mistake that roadmap language for parity with Meltwater or Syncly Social today. 3. Talkwalker Best for: teams that want NetBase Quid's enterprise scale plus non-gated speech-to-text and video-logo recognition, built into Blue Silk AI and included across every pricing tier rather than reserved for a top plan. Pricing: no official public pricing; third-party estimates run roughly $9,000-$13,000/year at the Core tier up to $150,000+/year at Enterprise (Source: ITQlick — Talkwalker Pricing, 2026 ). Its video and audio AI is described generically as covering "audio and video social media posts," rather than confirmed as purpose-built for TikTok, Reels, or Shorts specifically. 4. Meltwater Best for: teams that want media monitoring, social listening, and named-customer proof in one enterprise platform, with genuine short-form video transcription already shipped rather than promised. Pricing: no public list price; analyst estimates put median spend around $25,000/year, ranging from $6,000 at Starter to $150,000+ at Enterprise (Source: Vendr Marketplace — Meltwater, 2026 ). Meltwater's TikTok Marketing Partners integration adds real TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram video transcription via keyframe analysis and speech-to-text, and its named beauty and consumer customer stories — Shiseido, Yves Rocher, Bon Parfumeur — give it the strongest combination of proof and shipped video AI in this comparison outside Syncly. 5. Sprinklr Best for: enterprise teams that want listening, customer service, marketing, and advertising bundled into a single platform of five separately licensed modules, rather than a dedicated consumer-intelligence tool. Pricing: enterprise contracts start around $50,000/year, with a median near $129,380/year; Sprinklr discontinued its self-serve program entirely as of April 30, 2026, moving to enterprise-only sales, with implementation running an additional $25,000-$150,000 (Source: Chatarmin — Sprinklr Pricing, 2026 ). No confirmed video-content-transcription capability was found in this research — its AI+ Studio focuses on comment summarization and multi-LLM orchestration, not watching or listening to video itself. 6. Synthesio, an Ipsos company Best for: teams already inside or adjacent to the Ipsos market-research ecosystem that want NetBase Quid-tier social listening plus a credible, research-grade video-intelligence layer. Pricing: no public list price; enterprise custom quotes based on usage and data volume. The genuinely surprising finding here: as of January 2026, Synthesio and ViralMoment became official platform partners, adding real scene and logo recognition, comment and caption analysis, and TikTok transcripts across YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram (Source: Synthesio — Ipsos Synthesio & ViralMoment Partnership, 2026 ). It's third-party-sourced rather than natively built — but real and shipped, which makes Synthesio the honest exception to treating this whole tier as blind to video. 7. Digimind, now Onclusive Social Best for: budget-conscious teams that want an enterprise-style consumer-intelligence tool without NetBase Quid's or Brandwatch's price tag. Pricing: no public list price; third-party estimates start around $6,000-$20,000/year depending on seats and modules (Source: Prospeo — Onclusive Social Pricing, 2026 ). No confirmed video-transcription capability was found, and no independently located named case study — the same pattern found for its parent company, Onclusive, when researching Determ alternatives. 8. YouScan Best for: budget-conscious teams that specifically want image recognition — YouScan claims up to 80% more brand mentions detected than text-only monitoring — without an enterprise price tag attached. Pricing: Starter plans from $499/month billed annually, with Unlimited tiers adding visual insights, audience insights, and API access as programs scale (Source: YouScan — Pricing, 2026 ). YouScan also offers audio monitoring for spoken mentions inside YouTube videos specifically — a real, if platform-limited, video/audio capability at a fraction of the price of NetBase Quid, Brandwatch, or Sprinklr. That audio coverage is confirmed for YouTube only, not for TikTok or Instagram Reels, so don't treat it as equivalent to cross-platform video coverage. How the best NetBase Quid alternatives compare Tool Best For Starting Price Video/Visual Capability Key Differentiator Syncly Social Video-native brand and consumer-insights teams Custom (book a demo) Native — audio transcription + on-screen visual detection, all tiers Untagged mention detection across 10+ platforms by default NetBase Quid (Quid) Enterprise brand tracking, network visualization, predictive analytics ~$20K-$50K+/yr (quote-only) None confirmed — text/metadata + Feb 2026 AI-agent query layer Network and topic visualization; genuinely strong but text-first Brandwatch Enterprise consumer intelligence, deepest historical archive Custom Roadmapped, not shipped 1.7 trillion historical conversations back to 2010 Talkwalker Enterprise consumer intelligence ~$9K-$150K+/yr Non-gated speech-to-text + video-logo recognition (platform-generic) Blue Silk AI, no tier-gating Meltwater Enterprise PR and social media intelligence ~$6K-$150K+/yr Genuine TikTok video transcription (Marketing Partners) Strongest named-customer roster researched in this cluster Sprinklr Enterprise all-in-one CX suite ~$50K+/yr (enterprise-only) None confirmed Largest bundled suite (service, social, insights, marketing, advertising) Synthesio (Ipsos) Enterprise social intelligence + research-grade rigor Custom Real, via January 2026 ViralMoment partnership The genuinely surprising video-capable exception in this tier Digimind (Onclusive Social) Budget-tier enterprise consumer intelligence ~$6K-$20K/yr None confirmed Cheapest true enterprise-style option in this set YouScan Budget-conscious image + partial video/audio recognition $499/mo Image recognition + YouTube-specific audio monitoring Lowest price point with any confirmed visual or audio capability Definitions Enterprise consumer and market intelligence platform : a category of tools — like NetBase Quid, Brandwatch, and Synthesio — that ingest large-scale social, news, review, and market data primarily as text and metadata to power brand tracking, competitive analysis, and predictive trend forecasting for global consumer brands. This is distinct from a video-native social listening platform , built specifically around understanding what's actually said and shown inside short-form video content across TikTok, Reels, and Shorts, rather than the words that happen to surround it. Key takeaways NetBase Quid is a genuinely well-regarded (4.3-4.6/5 across G2 and Capterra) enterprise platform for network visualization and predictive trend analysis — its main confirmed gaps are quote-only pricing with no self-serve tier and a scraper that its own users say misses posts on Instagram and TikTok. The company has rebranded twice since its 2020 merger — first to "Quid" in 2023, then to a "Q Platform" AI-agent architecture in February 2026 — but neither rebrand added video-content transcription or on-screen visual detection. The most surprising finding: Synthesio, an Ipsos company, quietly became video-capable via a January 2026 partnership with ViralMoment, making it the one enterprise NetBase Quid-tier peer in this comparison with real, shipped video intelligence besides Syncly. Named-customer proof varies widely even within this tier — Meltwater, Brandwatch, and NetBase Quid itself show strong, specific (if sometimes third-party-aggregated) results, while Sprinklr, Synthesio, Digimind, and YouScan have no independently located named case study. No platform in this comparison replaces another's core job — the real question is whether your gap is enterprise breadth and workflow, or genuine video-content understanding. There's no single universal "NetBase Quid replacement" here. NetBase Quid does its actual job — enterprise brand tracking, network visualization, and predictive market analysis — honestly and well. The real decision is which gap matters more: broader enterprise scale and bundled workflow tooling, which points toward Brandwatch, Sprinklr, or Meltwater depending on what else you need bundled in, or genuine video-content understanding, which is where NetBase Quid and most of this category still falls short. For teams evaluating that second question in more depth, this series has also compared Determ alternatives and Traackr alternatives . body_text: View All News Corning’s Strong Second-Quarter 2026 Financial Results(1) Demonstrate Progress on Recently Upgraded Springboard Plan July 28, 2026 CORNING, N.Y.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Corning Incorporated (NYSE: GLW) today announced its second-quarter 2026 results and provided its outlook for third-quarter 2026. News Summary: Year over year, Q2 core sales grew 17% to $4.74 billion. Core EPS grew 30% to $0.78. Optical Communications grew sales 32% to $2.07 billion, including a 65% increase in Enterprise Networks, with Gen AI product sales growing significantly faster. Solar grew sales 90% and completed an extended maintenance shutdown and equipment upgrade at Corning’s solar wafer facility. Management expects profitability to improve in Q3. Results demonstrate progress on upgraded Springboard Plan outlined at May 2026 investor day. The company’s internal Springboard Plan is to grow sales to an annualized run rate of $20 billion by the end of 2026, $30 billion by the end of 2028, and $40 billion by the end of 2030. Corning is entering a new phase of accelerating growth. The company expects to deliver a sales CAGR of 19% from Q4 2026 to Q4 2030 – while growing earnings faster than sales, with significantly higher returns on invested capital and substantially more free cash flow. Deep customer partnerships support Springboard growth opportunity. In Q2: Amazon announced a multiyear, multibillion-dollar agreement under which Corning will supply the optical fiber, cable, and connectivity solutions that power Amazon's expanding data center infrastructure across the United States. NVIDIA and Corning announced a long-term partnership in which Corning will expand its U.S.-based optical connectivity manufacturing capacity by 10x and expand its U.S. fiber production capacity by more than 50% to meet the accelerating demand driven by AI factory buildouts. In the third quarter, management expects core sales to grow approximately 16% year over year to a range of $4.9 billion to $5 billion and core EPS to grow approximately 28% year over year to a range of $0.85 to $0.89. (1) Second-quarter GAAP results: Sales were $4.51 billion, gross margin was 36.1%, operating margin was 15.5%, EPS was $0.64, and operating cash flow was $1.72 billion. Wendell P. Weeks, chairman, chief executive officer, and president, said, “In the second quarter, we delivered outstanding results, and we upgraded our Springboard Plan to grow sales to an annualized run rate of $20 billion by the end of 2026, $30 billion by the end of 2028, and $40 billion by the end of 2030. We’re entering a new phase of accelerating growth, and we expect to deliver a sales CAGR of 19% from Q4 2026 to Q4 2030 – while growing earnings faster than sales, with significantly higher returns on invested capital and substantially more free cash flow.” Weeks continued, “We continue to deepen our long-term customer partnerships with industry leaders, most recently with Amazon and NVIDIA. These partnerships provide strong proof points supporting our exciting Springboard Plan.” Ed Schlesinger, executive vice president and chief financial officer, said , “In the second quarter, we delivered our ninth consecutive quarter of year-over-year growth and continued to enhance our financial profile. We grew core sales 17% to $4.74 billion and core EPS 30% to $0.78. We expanded core gross margin 120 basis points to 39.6% and core operating margin 190 basis points to 20.9%. We also grew core ROIC 180 basis points to 14.9% and delivered strong adjusted free cash flow of $1.42 billion.” Schlesinger continued, “In the third quarter, we expect core sales to grow approximately 16% year over year to a range of $4.9 billion to $5 billion and core EPS to grow about 28% year over year to a range of $0.85 to $0.89. We also expect an improving impact on earnings from Solar starting in Q3 as our ramp continues, building toward a revenue stream of more than $3 billion with strong profit and cash flow. Overall, we are off to a great start on our upgraded Springboard plan to capture a new phase of accelerating growth.” Second-Quarter 2026 Financial Highlights: GAAP sales were $4.51 billion, up 17% year over year. Core sales were $4.74 billion, up 17% year over year. GAAP EPS was $0.64, up 19% year over year. Core EPS was $0.78, up 30% year over year. The difference between GAAP and core EPS principally reflects adjustments for hedged exposures, along with largely non-cash discrete tax items and restructuring and impairment charges. A complete quantitative reconciliation of these and other reconciling items appears in the tables accompanying this release. GAAP gross margin was 36.1%. title: Coherent Corp. Reports Third Quarter Fiscal 2025 Results
summary: May. 7, 2025. Coherent Corp. announced financial results today for its fiscal third quarter ended March, 31, 2025.
body_text: Q3 REVENUE OF $1.50B, INCREASED 24% Y/Y Q3 GAAP GROSS MARGIN OF 35.2%, INCREASED 491 bps Y/Y; Q3 NON-GAAP GROSS MARGIN OF 38.5%, INCREASED 490 bps Y/Y Q3 GAAP EPS OF $(0. 11), IMPROVED $0.18 Y/Y; Q3 NON-GAAP EPS OF $0.91, IMPROVED $0.53 Y/Y SAXONBURG, Pa., May 7, 2025 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) – Coherent Corp. (NYSE: COHR) (“Coherent,” “We,” or the “Company”), a global leader in materials, networking, and lasers, announced financial results today for its fiscal third quarter ended March 31, 2025. Revenue for the third quarter of fiscal 2025 was $1.50 billion, with GAAP gross margin of 35.2% and GAAP net loss of $0.11 per diluted share. On a non-GAAP basis, gross margin was 38.5% with net income per diluted share of $0.91. Jim Anderson, CEO, said, “We delivered strong growth and profitability in the March quarter with record revenue driven by another quarter of strong AI-related datacenter demand. We also introduced many new industry-leading optical networking products and technologies during the past quarter which position us well for long-term growth.” Sherri Luther, CFO, said, “Revenue growth and gross margin expansion drove a significant year-over-year improvement in our GAAP and non-GAAP EPS. We also paid down $136 million of our outstanding debt. Cash and capital allocation remain priorities for us, as we further improve operating leverage and efficiency, while continuing to make investments for the long-term growth of the company.
